pageDescription: Numbered specifications, MEC-01 to MEC-25, for answering challenges, sending a rule back for review when challenges against it keep winning, and halting a system while it is fixed.

changelog.summary: Rewrote the copy of MEC-01 to MEC-12 in plain sentences. A halt is described as containment while the rule is fixed and people are restored, upheld appeals are counted against the rule in MEC-06 and MEC-08, and MEC-04 is renamed Hard clock.
Filed every mechanism under the six safeguards, led the starters and role paths with challenges that reach the rule, and added that obligation to MEC-06.
Added citation metadata, mechanisms-level authorship details, and structured usage guidance.

filters.label: Capability
filters.description: What the system can do, kept apart from what it is permitted to do, and each widening approved.

filters.label: Authority
filters.description: Who granted the system its power, on what evidence, and when the grant ends.

filters.label: Evidence
filters.description: The records that show the reasons for switching it on are still true.

filters.description: Whether the service can run without the system, and what leaving it costs.

entries.title: MEC-20 Chain-boundary intervention
entries.summary: Give a chain of automated systems one stop control that reaches every step, so the chain is paused, measured, and held to account as one system.
cues: Enumerate the hops before you design the stop: a chain you cannot list is a chain you cannot halt.
One halt receipt for the chain, not a stop control per hop.
Measure the window the chain leaves a human after upstream latency has been spent.
steps: Enumerate every contributing delegation on the head grant in execution order.
Carry one intervention specification at the chain boundary whose exercise halts every hop.
Measure hop latencies from decision records and recompute the composed window whenever a hop's latency changes materially.
Move a chain with no measured human window to confirm mode at the boundary, or narrow it until a window exists.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-20 Chain-boundary intervention)
- Any consequential decision produced by a chain of delegations records the chain on the head grant, each hop resolving to a full delegation.
- The chain boundary carries one intervention specification, and exercising it halts every hop with a receipt covering the chain.
- A chain whose composed latency leaves no measured human window does not run unattended.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/chain-boundary-intervention
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-20)
- The interface exposes the chain boundary as a single stop surface, with the hops it covers named on the receipt.
- The composed window is displayed to the operator, not the per-hop clock each vendor promises.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-20)
[ ] Head grants enumerate their chains, and each hop resolves to a grant record.
[ ] Halt receipts cover the chain, and a halt test shows downstream hops did not continue.
[ ] Composed windows are measured from decision records, not from vendor estimates.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-20)
Trigger review when a chain decision could not be paused at the boundary, or when hops continued after the hop that was stopped.

artifacts.name: Chain enumeration
artifacts.purpose: The head grant's chain field, each id resolving to a grant record with mode and liability.

artifacts.name: Chain halt receipt
artifacts.purpose: One receipt per halt naming every hop stopped and the time it took.

artifacts.name: Composed-window measurement
artifacts.purpose: Measured upstream latency against the intervention window, per decision period.

example.title: One stop for a three-vendor claims chain
example.description: A payer's denial chain runs intake, scoring, and letter generation across three providers. The head grant lists all three hops; pausing the boundary stops all three, and the receipt names each. The composed window leaves the reviewer 90 seconds, so the chain runs in confirm mode at the boundary rather than unattended.

antiPatterns.title: Per-hop pause theater
antiPatterns.failure: Each hop exposes a stop control and each works, but downstream hops re-trigger the stopped one or continue on stale output, so the composed process never stops.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: One boundary intervention halts every hop, and the halt receipt covers the chain.
antiPatterns.warning: A chain that re-converges after an interruption was never stopped.

antiPatterns.title: Latency laundering
antiPatterns.failure: Each hop promises a sub-second review, so every hop's clock looks compliant and no one owes a human window.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The composed window is measured from decision records, and a chain without one cannot run unattended.
antiPatterns.warning: Parallel-sounding latency claims must be checked against whether the hops run in series.

entries.title: MEC-01 Decision log with dissent
entries.summary: Record each consequential decision with its decider, the dissent, the options ruled out, and a review date, so the people it affects and later reviewers can see why it was made.
cues: Record the options ruled out and why, not only the option chosen.
Record dissent in the dissenter's own words, with their role.
Set a review date and name the person who must hold the review.
steps: Log the decision, the decider, the options ruled out, and who was consulted in one record.
Add the dissent, and a plain-language summary that a person affected by the decision can read.
Set a review date and name the owner who must hold it.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-01 Decision log with dissent)
- Log every high-stakes change with its decider, the options ruled out, any dissent, and a review date with a named owner.
- Keep the log in the system of record, and link each entry from the audit and incident records that rely on it.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/decision-log
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-01)
- The receipt for each high-stakes automated decision carries the ID of the log entry for the rule it applied.
- The person decided about can reach a plain-language summary of that entry within two clicks of the outcome.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-01)
[ ] Each entry names the decider, the dissent or its recorded absence, and a review date.
[ ] Each entry has a plain-language summary that can be shared outside the team.
[ ] Reviews were held on their dates, and each one recorded an outcome.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-01)
Trigger review when a high-stakes change ships without a log entry or a dissent record, or when a review date passes with no review held.

artifacts.name: Decision record template
artifacts.purpose: Fields for the decision, the decider, the options ruled out, the dissent, the review date, and the review owner.

artifacts.name: Plain-language summary
artifacts.purpose: One paragraph saying what was decided and why, written for the person the decision affects.

artifacts.name: Review calendar entry
artifacts.purpose: The review date, its owner, and the evidence the review will check.

example.title: Recording a delayed launch
example.description: A benefits agency logs its decision to delay an automated renewal tool. The entry records two options ruled out and a dissent from the call-center lead: error rates on Spanish-language forms were never tested. The deputy director owns a review in six weeks, and the tool's appeal page links to the entry.

antiPatterns.title: Logs without dissent
antiPatterns.failure: The log records what was decided but not the options ruled out or who objected, so a later reviewer cannot tell what was weighed.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each entry records the options ruled out, the dissent, and a dated review with an owner.
antiPatterns.warning: An entry with no dissent is complete when it shows dissent was asked for and none was given.

antiPatterns.title: Reasons kept in private documents
antiPatterns.failure: The reasoning sits in a private document or chat thread, so the people affected and later reviewers cannot find it.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The entry lives in the system of record, and each decision receipt links to it.
antiPatterns.warning: Personal or security-sensitive details can be redacted, as long as the entry ID and the decision itself stay referenceable.

entries.title: MEC-02 Progressive consent prompts
entries.summary: Ask a person for each permission when the system needs it, with the reason and how to withdraw it. A withdrawal stops the automation it covered and does not cost them core service.
cues: Ask for each permission when it is needed, with the reason and how to withdraw it.
Show what changes for the person if they say no, before they choose.
Treat silence as no: if the person does not answer, the system does not collect or act.
steps: Split one large request into separate asks, each with its purpose, how long it lasts, and how to withdraw it.
Before each ask, show what the person loses by declining, and keep the withdrawal control in the same place afterward.
Add a pause control that stops automated use of the person's data and routes their case to staff, with no loss of core service.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-02 Progressive consent prompts)
- Ask for consent in stages, each with a stated purpose, duration, and way to withdraw.
- When consent is refused or withdrawn, the covered collection or automation stops, and the person keeps core service.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/progressive-consent
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-02)
- Each consent request states its purpose, how long it lasts, and how to withdraw it.
- The withdrawal control stays visible after consent, and using it does not remove access to core or safety features.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-02)
[ ] The consent record lists each ask with its purpose, duration, and withdrawal path.
[ ] Withdrawal instructions match across the interface, email, and help pages.
[ ] Production tests show that a withdrawal stops the covered processing and stays in effect.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-02)
Trigger review when a withdrawal fails or is ignored, or when automation restarts without the person's renewed consent.

artifacts.name: Consent journey map
artifacts.purpose: Each ask in order, with its purpose, duration, and withdrawal path.

artifacts.name: Withdrawal wording
artifacts.purpose: Short text on how to withdraw, used the same way in the interface, email, and help pages.

artifacts.name: Pause control checklist
artifacts.purpose: Confirms before release that each step has a pause that stops automated use and routes the case to staff.

example.title: Staging consent in a tax-filing assistant
example.description: A tax-filing assistant asks to read last year's return only when the person requests a refund estimate, and says the estimate will be rougher without it. It asks again, separately, before pre-filling forms. A pause control on every screen stops automated use and hands the session to a staff preparer.

antiPatterns.title: One-shot consent bundles
antiPatterns.failure: Every permission is requested on the first screen, with no reason, duration, or way to withdraw each one.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each permission is asked for when it is needed, with its reason, duration, and withdrawal path.
antiPatterns.warning: A single ask is acceptable when it covers only what the core service cannot run without, and says so.

antiPatterns.title: Opt-out that does not stick
antiPatterns.failure: The toggle turns off, but the automation keeps running or restarts after an update without telling the person.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: A withdrawal stops the covered processing, is logged, and is confirmed to the person on screen.
antiPatterns.warning: Processing the service cannot run without, such as fraud checks on a payment, can continue if it was disclosed before the person chose.

entries.title: MEC-03 Maintenance windowing
entries.summary: Make changes to a decision system in published windows, each with a named owner, a rollback plan, and notice to the people the change affects.
cues: Name an owner for each window and the result that counts as done.
Tell the people a change affects what will differ and when, with more notice for higher-risk changes.
State what happens to a case when a dependency fails, such as holding it or routing it to a person.
steps: Set each window with an owner, the result that counts as done, and the person who can order a rollback.
Before the window opens, notify the people the change affects, with lead time set by the change's risk.
List each dependency and its fallback when it fails, and test each fallback before the window opens.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-03 Maintenance windowing)
- Publish maintenance windows, each with a named owner, the result that counts as done, and the person who can order a rollback.
- Set a minimum notice period for each risk tier, and notify the people affected before any change ships.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/maintenance-windowing
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-03)
- Each change ticket names its window and its owner.
- During a window, people affected can see status updates and which fallback the system is using.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-03)
[ ] The window calendar lists each window's owner, coverage hours, and the result that counts as done.
[ ] Each change was announced with the lead time its risk tier requires.
[ ] Each dependency has a fallback, with the date it was last tested.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-03)
Trigger review when a change ships outside a window, without notice, or without a tested rollback.

artifacts.name: Window calendar
artifacts.purpose: Each window with its owner, coverage hours, and the result that counts as done.

artifacts.name: Notice templates
artifacts.purpose: Prewritten notices for high-, medium-, and low-risk changes, with the lead time and sender for each.

artifacts.name: Fallback table
artifacts.purpose: Each dependency, what the system does when it fails, and who is paged.

example.title: A two-week window for a screening model update
example.description: A housing authority updates its tenant-screening model in a two-week window owned by the data team lead, who can roll back on her own authority if the denial rate moves more than two points. Applicants with pending cases get notice ten days ahead. If the credit-data feed fails, new applications go to a caseworker instead of being scored.

antiPatterns.title: Maintenance without owners
antiPatterns.failure: A window is published with no owner and no one named to order a rollback, so a bad change stays in place while people argue about who decides.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each window names an owner, the result that counts as done, and who can order a rollback.
antiPatterns.warning: Two owners can share a window when the record says which one decides on rollback.

antiPatterns.title: Silent maintenance
antiPatterns.failure: Changes ship without notice, so people meet new behavior with no warning and cannot tell an error from a change.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The people affected get notice with lead time set by risk tier, and the fallback is named.
antiPatterns.warning: An emergency fix can ship before notice goes out, as long as the notice and an after-action record follow.

entries.title: MEC-04 Hard clock
entries.summary: Give every state a case can occupy a declared maximum duration, so no one waits in pending forever. At the limit, the case fails safe or goes to a named person who must decide.
cues: Declare the maximum duration of each state before people commit to the process.
Decide in advance whether expiry fails safe or escalates to a named human.
Review the timeout log each month with the named owner of the clock.
steps: Inventory every state a request can occupy and set a maximum duration for each.
Wire expiry to a fail-safe resolution or a human escalation with a named owner.
Show the declared duration in the interface and log every breach for monthly review.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-04 Hard clock)
- Every automated process declares a maximum duration and a human escalation path when it is exceeded.
- Expired processes fail safe and keep the person's progress, so they can re-enter without starting over.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/hard-clock
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-04)
- The declared maximum duration is visible before a person commits to the process.
- Timeout events emit a receipt with the state, elapsed time, and escalation owner.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-04)
[ ] Each system state has a documented maximum duration.
[ ] Timeout logs record expiry, resolution, and escalation owner.
[ ] Monthly reviews were held by the clock's named owner.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-04)
Trigger review when a state exceeds its declared duration without failing safe or escalating.

artifacts.name: Timeout log
artifacts.purpose: Each expiry, how it resolved, and who it went to, for the monthly review with the clock's owner.

example.title: Bounding a manual review queue
example.description: A payments team caps identity review at 72 hours, shows the cap at submission, and routes anything still pending at expiry to a named reviewer who must release or refuse the hold.

antiPatterns.title: Pending with no ceiling
antiPatterns.failure: A state has a target but no maximum, so slow cases accumulate with no escalation.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Every state declares a maximum duration and a resolution at expiry.
antiPatterns.warning: A state the person controls, such as a draft they have not submitted, needs no ceiling.

antiPatterns.title: Clock without a resolution
antiPatterns.failure: The timer expires and emits an alert, but the request stays in the same state.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Expiry moves the request to a fail-safe outcome or to a named person who can change its state.
antiPatterns.warning: An internal state that holds no person's request, such as a batch retry, can end in an alert alone.

entries.title: MEC-05 Kill switch for runaway automation
entries.searchTitle: AI kill switch pattern for runaway automation
entries.metaDescription: A pre-authorized halt for an AI or other automated system: a named roster, harm-indicator triggers, a time-to-halt target, and restoration for those harmed.
entries.summary: Give a named roster pre-authorized power to halt an automated system when harm indicators fire. The halt contains harm while the rule's owner fixes the rule and the people harmed are restored.
cues: Set halt triggers on harm indicators, such as a spike in upheld appeals, and on reports from frontline staff.
Name who may fire the switch, and protect them from retaliation for using it.
Plan what follows the halt: the rule's owner changes the rule, and the people harmed are restored.
steps: Mark the points where the automation can stop, and what happens to cases in flight at each one.
Set the triggers that fire a halt, a time-to-halt target for each, and the roster that may fire it.
Drill the full sequence: halt, notify the people affected, send the rule to its owner, restore the people harmed, then resume.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-05 Kill switch for runaway automation)
- Keep a pre-authorized halt path with a named roster, and protect anyone on it from retaliation for using it.
- Publish halt triggers tied to harm indicators, each with a time-to-halt target.
- Resume only after the rule's owner records a fix and a dated plan exists to restore the people harmed.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/kill-switch
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-05)
- Operators can fire the kill switch in one step from the monitoring view.
- Each halt emits a receipt naming who fired it, the trigger, the cases held, and the restoration checklist.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-05)
[ ] The runbook names the authorized roster and the triggers.
[ ] Drill logs show measured time-to-halt against the target.
[ ] Each real halt links to the rule change that followed and a record of the people restored.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-05)
Trigger review when a time-to-halt target is missed, the kill switch is unavailable, or automation resumes with no recorded fix and no plan to restore the people harmed.

artifacts.name: Kill switch runbook
artifacts.purpose: Triggers, the authorized roster, and the notice sent to people whose cases were held.

artifacts.name: Restoration checklist
artifacts.purpose: Each person harmed, what they are owed, and the date each was restored.

artifacts.name: After-action record
artifacts.purpose: What fired the switch, what the rule's owner changed, and whether the trigger threshold moved.

example.title: Halting a disconnection notice run
example.description: After a meter-data change, a utility's billing rule flags three times the usual number of homes for disconnection, and upheld disputes spike. The on-call operator halts disconnection notices in four minutes. The rule's owner fixes how the rule reads the new meter format. The 310 households already notified get a withdrawal letter and a fee refund. Then notices resume.

antiPatterns.title: Kill switch without rehearsal
antiPatterns.failure: A halt path exists on paper but has never been fired, so the first real use finds missing permissions and stale contacts.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The halt is drilled, and each drill records time-to-halt against the target.
antiPatterns.warning: A tabletop drill can stand in where a live halt would harm people, if the log records what it could not test.

antiPatterns.title: Single-point approval
antiPatterns.failure: Only one person can fire the halt, so at night or during their leave nobody can stop the system.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: A named roster can fire the halt at any hour, without sign-off and without retaliation.
antiPatterns.warning: A small team can run a primary and a secondary, if the roster shows who covers each hour.

entries.title: MEC-06 Appeal paths inside the UI
entries.summary: Put an appeal next to each automated decision, so the person decided about can dispute it and get a human answer by a stated date. Upheld appeals count against the rule.
cues: Say who reviews appeals and the date by which they will answer.
Pre-fill the decision and its reasons, so the person does not have to rebuild the case.
Count upheld appeals by the rule that produced them, not only in total.
steps: Place the appeal next to the decision, showing who reviews it and the answer date.
Pre-fill the decision, its reason code, and the data used, so the person adds only what is wrong.
Count upheld appeals by rule and send the count to the rule's owner. A set number sends the rule back for review (MEC-14 Policy review triggers).
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-06 Appeal paths inside the UI)
- Provide an appeal channel inside the product, with a published answer date and a named reviewer role.
- Count upheld appeals by the rule that produced them, and send the count to the rule's owner. A set number sends the rule back for review.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/appeal-paths
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-06)
- Every appeal returns a receipt with the answer date and the role that will answer.
- The appeal is one step from the decision screen.
- Each upheld appeal records the reason code of the rule it overturned.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-06)
[ ] The appeal form pre-fills the decision and its reason code.
[ ] The reviewer roster and the escalation path are written down.
[ ] The outcome log records each appeal's answer time and result.
[ ] Upheld appeals are counted by rule, and the count reaches the rule's owner.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-06)
Trigger review when appeals pass their published answer date, or when a rule reaches its upheld-appeal threshold and its owner has not reviewed it.

artifacts.name: Appeal intake form
artifacts.purpose: Asks only for what the person must add, with the decision and its reason code filled in.

artifacts.name: Reviewer roster
artifacts.purpose: Who answers appeals, the hours covered, and where an unanswered appeal goes next.

artifacts.name: Outcome log
artifacts.purpose: Each appeal's result, the time taken, and the rule an upheld appeal counted against.

example.title: Adding appeals to a credit-limit tool
example.description: A lender puts a “Dispute this limit” link beside each automated credit-limit cut, with the reason code filled in and a ten-day answer date. In the first quarter, 62 of 80 upheld appeals trace to one income-verification rule. The count reaches that rule's owner, and because it passes the threshold of 50, the rule goes back for review.

antiPatterns.title: Appeal link buried
antiPatterns.failure: Appeals exist, but only in help pages or a separate portal, so few of the people affected find them.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The appeal sits next to the decision, with the answer date shown.
antiPatterns.warning: A help-center route works for rare decisions if the decision notice links straight to it.

antiPatterns.title: Appeals without feedback
antiPatterns.failure: Disputes are collected, but the person gets no receipt, no answer date, and no outcome.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Every appeal returns a receipt and an answer date, and the outcome is logged.
antiPatterns.warning: Answer dates can vary with case complexity if the notice states the range and the log tracks it.

antiPatterns.title: Appeals that only fix cases
antiPatterns.failure: Each upheld appeal corrects one decision. The rule that produced it stays, and the next person meets the same error.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Upheld appeals are counted by rule, and a set number obliges the rule's owner to revise it or publish why not.
antiPatterns.warning: An appeal upheld because of a data-entry error in one case need not count against the rule, if that reason is recorded.

entries.title: MEC-07 Accountability latency tracker
entries.summary: Measure the time from a trigger firing to a named person intervening, halting the system, and restoring the people harmed, so the risk owner sees every missed target.
cues: Record each intervention, halt, and restore with a timestamp, the person who acted, and the trigger.
Publish a latency target for each, next to the time-to-halt target.
Link each missed target to a repair log entry that says what changed.
Feed missed targets into the transition rules on authority grants, so a breach can move a grant to review_required.
steps: Define the records: intervention, halt, and restore events, each with a timestamp, the actor, and the trigger.
Build one view of median and worst-case latency, with each missed target marked, for the operator and the risk owner.
At each incident review, the risk owner compares latency to target and updates the runbook.
Wire missed targets to the grant transition rules, so an observation can change the grant's state (MEC-13 Authority grant register).
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-07 Accountability latency tracker)
- Record intervention, halt, and restore times with the person who acted, the trigger, and the system.
- Publish accountability latency targets in the incident runbook.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/accountability-latency-tracker
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-07)
- The monitoring view shows accountability latency next to time-to-halt.
- Each intervention emits a receipt linked to the repair log and the escalation owner.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-07)
[ ] Intervention, halt, and restore events are recorded with timestamps.
[ ] Reports show median and worst-case accountability latency.
[ ] Incident reviews record latency against target and what was changed.
[ ] Missed targets move the grant's state and produce a reconsideration record.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-07)
Trigger review when accountability latency misses a published target, or when the events needed to measure it were not recorded.

artifacts.name: Event definitions
artifacts.purpose: Names and required fields for intervention, halt, and restore records.

artifacts.name: Latency report
artifacts.purpose: Latency trends with each missed target marked, prepared for the incident review.

artifacts.name: Latency response runbook
artifacts.purpose: Who acts on a missed target, where it escalates, and what they change.

example.title: Tracking override time during a claims surge
example.description: A car insurer records each time a reviewer overrides an automated claim denial. During a surge of storm-damage claims, median time to override rises from 20 minutes to 6 hours. The miss is logged against the target, the denial grant moves to review_required, and the risk owner adds two reviewers to the night roster.

antiPatterns.title: Latency tracked without owners
antiPatterns.failure: The times are recorded, but no one is named to act when a target is missed.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each target names the owner who acts on a miss and where it escalates.
antiPatterns.warning: Two teams can share a target if the record says which one acts first.

antiPatterns.title: Latency without repair links
antiPatterns.failure: Missed targets are logged but never tied to a fix, so the same delay comes back.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Every missed target links to a repair log entry that says what changed.
antiPatterns.warning: A miss caused by a one-time outside event, such as a regional power outage, can close with a recorded reason instead of a fix.

entries.title: MEC-08 Contestation APIs
entries.summary: Let the person decided about, or someone acting for them, challenge a decision through a published API and get an answer by a deadline. An upheld challenge changes the decision.
cues: Publish a stable contract: the inputs, the obliged responder, and the answer deadline.
Return a receipt on filing with a challenge ID, the status, and where it goes if the deadline passes.
Make an upheld challenge change the decision's state, with no manual re-entry.

Carry the standing-register fields in the contract: who may challenge, what they may challenge, admissible evidence, the obliged responder, the deadline, the standard of review, and the transitions a successful challenge can produce.
steps: Define an authenticated challenge endpoint with the evidence fields the standing register admits.
Send status updates to the challenger, tied to the decision record, until the challenge is answered.
Write each upheld challenge to the decision's state and log the remedy. Count upheld challenges by rule and send the count to the rule's owner (MEC-14 Policy review triggers).
Publish the standing register next to the API, so a challenger can see before filing who must answer, by when, against what standard, and what an upheld challenge can change.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-08 Contestation APIs)
- Publish a challenge API with an obliged responder and an answer deadline, and let an upheld challenge change the decision's state without manual re-entry.
- Publish the standing register: who may challenge what, the admissible evidence, the responder, the deadline, and the standard of review.
- Count upheld challenges by the rule that produced the decision, and send the count to the rule's owner.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/contestation-apis
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-08)
- Each challenge returns a receipt naming the responder, the deadline, and where it escalates if the deadline passes.
- An upheld challenge updates the decision's state and notifies the person it concerns.
- Each upheld challenge records the reason code of the rule it overturned.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-08)
[ ] The API contract and its authentication policy are versioned.
[ ] Receipts carry timestamps, the responder, and the escalation path.
[ ] State-change logs link each upheld challenge to the decision it changed and the remedy given.
[ ] Upheld challenges are counted by rule, and the count reaches each rule's owner.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-08)
Trigger review when an upheld challenge has not changed the decision's state by the deadline.

artifacts.name: Contestation API spec
artifacts.purpose: Endpoints, required fields, and the receipt returned on filing.

artifacts.name: Receipt and status schema
artifacts.purpose: The status updates a challenger receives, and the escalation details each one carries.

artifacts.name: State-change log
artifacts.purpose: Each upheld challenge, the decision it reversed, and the remedy given.

artifacts.name: Standing register
artifacts.purpose: Who may challenge what, with admissible evidence, obliged responder, deadline, standard of review, and possible transitions.

example.title: A challenge API for eligibility reversals
example.description: A benefits platform lets legal aid groups file challenges for their clients through an API. Each filing returns a receipt naming the eligibility unit as responder and a 72-hour deadline. When a reviewer upholds a challenge, eligibility updates with no re-entry, and the upheld count for that rule goes to its owner.

antiPatterns.title: Challenges that change nothing
antiPatterns.failure: Challenges are accepted and even upheld, but the decision record never changes, so the person stays denied.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: An upheld challenge writes to the decision's state through the same workflow that made the decision.
antiPatterns.warning: A manual update is acceptable when the log shows it landed before the deadline.

antiPatterns.title: Channel without standing
antiPatterns.failure: The API accepts submissions but never says who is entitled to a response, by when, or against what standard it will be judged.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The contract names the responder, the deadline, the standard of review, and the transitions a successful challenge can produce.
antiPatterns.warning: A broad standing rule is fine; leaving standing unstated is not.

entries.title: MEC-09 Burden dashboards
entries.summary: Measure the time, steps, documents, and waiting a person spends to use or correct the system, split by group, and send each breach to a named owner.
cues: Report burden next to outcome and response-time figures, not in a separate report.
Split burden by group and channel, such as language, disability access, and phone versus web, so a gap between groups shows.
Treat a threshold breach as an incident with a named owner and a fix date.
steps: Define the measures: minutes, steps, documents requested, waiting time, and handoffs, each with a threshold.
Report each measure by group and channel, with the median and the 90th percentile.
Send each breach to the owner of the step that caused it, with a date for the fix.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-09 Burden dashboards)
- Publish burden measures and thresholds for each high-stakes system.
- Assign each threshold breach to a named owner with a fix date.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/burden-dashboards
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-09)
- Burden reports show median and 90th-percentile figures by group and channel.
- A threshold breach opens a fix task with a named owner.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-09)
[ ] Each burden measure is defined and recorded the same way in every channel.
[ ] Reports split burden by group and channel, and include the appeal path.
[ ] Each breach links to a fix task, its owner, and the measure after the fix.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-09)
Trigger review when a burden breach passes its fix date with no fix, or when one group exceeds a threshold that the overall figure does not.

artifacts.name: Burden measure definitions
artifacts.purpose: What each measure counts, where the data comes from, and its threshold.

artifacts.name: Burden report
artifacts.purpose: Trends by group and channel, with each breach marked.

artifacts.name: Burden fix log
artifacts.purpose: Each breach, its owner, the fix made, and the measure afterward.

example.title: Publishing a monthly burden report
example.description: A city permits office reports that appealing a parking-permit denial takes a median of 40 minutes and three documents online, but three hours and five documents by phone, where most callers are over 70. The phone gap is logged as a breach, and the intake manager owns a fix due in 60 days.

antiPatterns.title: Burden tracking without action
antiPatterns.failure: Burden is measured and charted, but no one is named to fix a breach, so the figures grow with no response.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each breach goes to a named owner with a fix date.
antiPatterns.warning: A small team can rotate the owner role, if the record shows who held it for each breach.

antiPatterns.title: Averages that hide a group
antiPatterns.failure: Burden is reported only as one overall figure, so a group carrying far more of it, such as phone callers or people filing in a second language, does not show.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Burden is reported by group and channel, with the worst-off group's figure beside the overall one.
antiPatterns.warning: Groups too small to report without identifying people can be merged, if the merged figure is labeled.

entries.title: MEC-10 Reversibility audit logs
entries.summary: Record whether each consequential action can be undone, by whom, and how fast, so a person wrongly decided about can be put back. Require a stated reason for any that cannot.
cues: Record reversibility status, who can reverse, and the reason, for every high-stakes action type.
Log each reversal attempt with the time it took to restore the person to where they were.
Report the share of irreversible actions to the risk owner, with the reason for each.
steps: Tag each action type as reversible, reversible within a time limit, or irreversible, with the reason.
Log every reversal attempt with timestamps, the outcome, and whether the person was fully restored.
At each review, the risk owner accepts each irreversibility reason on the record or orders a way to reverse the action.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-10 Reversibility audit logs)
- Keep a log of each high-stakes action type's reversibility status, who can reverse it, and the reason for any irreversibility.
- Record every reversal attempt with its time to restore and whether the person was fully restored.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/reversibility-audit-logs
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-10)
- Each decision record shows its reversibility status and who can reverse it.
- Each reversal attempt emits a receipt with timestamps and the outcome.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-10)
[ ] Reversibility status is recorded for every high-stakes action type.
[ ] Reversal attempts are logged with time to restore.
[ ] Each irreversibility reason names who accepted it and when it was last reviewed.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-10)
Trigger review when an action has no reversibility record, a reversal exceeds its target time, or an action recorded as reversible could not be reversed.

artifacts.name: Reversibility register
artifacts.purpose: Each action type with its status, who can reverse it, and the reason.

artifacts.name: Reversal attempt log
artifacts.purpose: Each attempt, its outcome, and the time taken to restore the person.

artifacts.name: Irreversibility review record
artifacts.purpose: Each irreversible action type, the reason accepted, who accepted it, and when.

example.title: Logging reversals in a claims system
example.description: A health insurer logs every reversal of an automated claim denial. Most reverse within two days. Denials that set off a collections referral take 45 days, because the referral cannot be recalled automatically. The risk owner records this as a reversibility gap and orders a recall path.

antiPatterns.title: Implicit irreversibility
antiPatterns.failure: Actions are treated as final with no stated reason, so no one asks whether they could be undone.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each action type has a recorded reversibility status and reason, reviewed by the risk owner.
antiPatterns.warning: An action can be irreversible for a short window, such as a payment in transit, if the window and its end are recorded.

antiPatterns.title: Reversed in the record only
antiPatterns.failure: The decision record flips back, but what it set off, such as a debt referral or a letter to an employer, stays in place.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: A reversal is complete when each downstream consequence is withdrawn and the person is told.
antiPatterns.warning: A consequence that cannot be withdrawn, such as a letter already read, can close with a correction sent to the same recipient.

entries.title: MEC-11 Escalation SLAs
entries.summary: Publish a deadline for a human answer when a person escalates an automated decision, and staff to meet it. A missed deadline triggers a stated fallback, such as pausing the decision.
cues: Publish each escalation deadline with the role that must answer and the hours covered.
Check each deadline against the staffing roster before publishing it.
Decide in advance what a missed deadline does, such as pausing or reversing the decision until a person answers.
steps: Define escalation tiers, each with a deadline and what the responder may change.
Track each escalation against its deadline, with a receipt to the person and an alert before the deadline passes.
The escalation owner reviews missed deadlines and either adds staff or narrows the cases the system decides alone (MEC-23 Challenge load ledger).
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-11 Escalation SLAs)
- Publish escalation deadlines and the role that must answer at each tier.
- Define what a missed deadline does, such as pausing or reversing the decision until a person answers.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/escalation-slas
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-11)
- Each escalation receipt shows the deadline and the role that must answer.
- A missed deadline triggers the stated fallback with no manual step.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-11)
[ ] Escalation deadlines and responder roles are published.
[ ] Missed deadlines, and the fallback each triggered, are logged.
[ ] The staffing roster covers every hour a deadline runs.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-11)
Trigger review when missed deadlines exceed the set threshold, or when a missed deadline did not trigger its fallback.

artifacts.name: Escalation deadline table
artifacts.purpose: Each tier, its deadline, and what the responder may change.

artifacts.name: Coverage roster
artifacts.purpose: Who is on duty for each hour a deadline runs.

artifacts.name: Missed-deadline log
artifacts.purpose: Each missed deadline and the fallback it triggered.

example.title: A 24-hour deadline for frozen accounts
example.description: A payments company publishes a 24-hour deadline for a human answer when a customer disputes an automated account freeze. Staff cover nights and weekends. If the deadline passes, the account unfreezes provisionally and stays open until a reviewer decides.

antiPatterns.title: Escalation without coverage
antiPatterns.failure: A deadline is published, but no one is rostered nights or weekends, so an escalation filed Friday evening waits until Monday.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The roster covers every hour the deadline runs.
antiPatterns.warning: Office-hours coverage is acceptable if the deadline counts only those hours and the notice says so.

antiPatterns.title: Escalation to someone who cannot decide
antiPatterns.failure: The escalation reaches a person who can explain the decision but not change it, so the deadline is met and nothing moves.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each tier's responder can pause or reverse the decision within that tier's scope.
antiPatterns.warning: A first tier that only gathers facts is fine if it hands the case to a tier that can decide within the same deadline.

entries.title: MEC-12 Stoppability testing
entries.summary: Before launch and after each major change, test that the people authorized to halt the system can do it within the target time, and that cases in flight stop safely.
cues: Run a halt drill before launch and after each major change.
Write down who can halt, how, and the target time to halt.
Log each drill's result, and close each gap before release.
steps: Write test scenarios for each halt path (MEC-05 Kill switch for runaway automation): the trigger, the person who halts, and the cases in flight.
Run each drill, timing the halt and checking that cases in flight land in a safe state and can be restored.
Report the results to the risk owner, and hold the release until each gap is closed.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-12 Stoppability testing)
- Run halt drills before launch and after each major change.
- Publish time-to-halt targets and the roles authorized to halt.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/stoppability-testing
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-12)
- Each drill logs time-to-halt, the state cases were left in, and whether they were restored.
- The launch gate checks that drills ran and their gaps are closed.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-12)
[ ] Drill logs record time-to-halt and the result.
[ ] The people authorized to halt are named.
[ ] Each gap a drill found is tracked to a fix.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-12)
Trigger review when a drill is skipped, a time-to-halt target is missed, or a real halt fails in a way the drills did not test.

artifacts.name: Stoppability test plan
artifacts.purpose: Scenarios, triggers, the person who halts, and the target time for each.

artifacts.name: Drill log
artifacts.purpose: Each drill's time-to-halt, the state cases were left in, and the restoration steps taken.

artifacts.name: Launch gate checklist
artifacts.purpose: Confirms drills ran and their gaps closed before deployment.

example.title: A halt drill before automated approvals go live
example.description: A benefits team drills a halt on its automated approval flow a week before launch. The on-call operator stops approvals in 3 minutes against a 5-minute target, but 40 approvals already in the queue are sent anyway. Launch waits until queued approvals hold at the halt.

antiPatterns.title: Stoppability assumed, not tested
antiPatterns.failure: The team relies on a documented halt path that no one has run.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Halt drills run before launch and after major changes, and log their results.
antiPatterns.warning: A drill in a staging copy counts if it uses the production halt controls and permissions.

antiPatterns.title: Testing the switch, not the stop
antiPatterns.failure: The drill confirms the switch flips, but queued jobs and downstream systems keep acting on decisions already made.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The drill checks what happened to queued cases and downstream systems after the halt.
antiPatterns.warning: Work already finished downstream can stay in place if the drill shows each item can be reversed.

entries.title: MEC-13 Authority grant register
entries.summary: Hold every delegated authority as a stateful record with provenance, scope, evidence basis, expiry, revocation conditions, and state history.
cues: Give each grant a state, not a boolean: proposed, allowed, review_required, suspended, revoked.
Record what the grant rests on, who issued it, and what would end it.
Expose the register to the decision log so an action can name the grant it ran under.
steps: Enumerate the authorities the system currently exercises and write one record per grant.
Add provenance, scope, evidence basis, expiry, and revocation conditions to each record.
Append every state change to the grant's history and link the register to the decision log.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-13 Authority grant register)
- Maintain a register of delegated authorities with issuer, scope, evidence basis, expiry, and revocation conditions.
- Record every grant state change with its reason and reviewer, and expose the register to the decision log.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/authority-grant-register
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-13)
- Each consequential action names the grant identifier and grant state it ran under.
- Grants past expiry move to review_required and are refused until a reviewer renews them.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-13)
[ ] Every exercised authority has a register entry with issuer and scope.
[ ] Grants carry an expiry and stated revocation conditions.
[ ] State history shows who changed each grant and on what basis.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-13)
Trigger review when an action runs under a grant that is missing, expired, or not in the allowed state.

artifacts.name: Grant record template
artifacts.purpose: Fields for issuer, holder, scope, evidence basis, expiry, revocation conditions, and state.

artifacts.name: State transition table
artifacts.purpose: The permitted moves between grant states and who may make each one.

artifacts.name: Renewal calendar
artifacts.purpose: Upcoming expiries with the reviewer responsible for each renewal decision.

example.title: Registering an agent's refund authority
example.description: A support platform records the agent's refund authority as a grant with a value ceiling, an evidence basis in the last accuracy review, a 90-day expiry, and revocation on any confirmed mis-refund; the refund endpoint reads the grant state before acting.

antiPatterns.title: Permissions as config
antiPatterns.failure: Authority lives in a role file or feature flag with no issuer, basis, or expiry, so widening it is a deploy rather than a decision.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Authority lives in a register where each grant names its issuer, basis, expiry, and revocation conditions.
antiPatterns.warning: Config can still enforce the grant; the register is the record of why the config says what it says.

antiPatterns.title: Register without state
antiPatterns.failure: Grants are documented once and never move, so an expired or contested grant reads the same as a current one.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each grant carries a current state and an appended history of transitions.
antiPatterns.warning: A stable grant is fine; what matters is that the register can show it was reviewed and left in place.

entries.title: MEC-14 Policy review triggers
entries.summary: Give every policy an expiry date and named triggers that send the authority grants that depend on it back to review when conditions change.
cues: Write down the propositions a policy assumes, not only the rule it states.
Name the observation that should reopen the policy, and the threshold that counts.
Link each policy to the grants that rest on it so a fired trigger can reach them.
steps: Give each policy a version, an assumption list, an expiry, and named review triggers.
Link grants to the policies they depend on so the dependency is queryable.
On a fired trigger or a passed expiry, move dependent grants to review_required and notify the reviewer.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-14 Policy review triggers)
- Every policy record carries a version, stated assumptions, an expiry, and named review triggers.
- A fired trigger or a passed expiry moves dependent authority grants to review_required.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/policy-review-triggers
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-14)
- Policy records expose the grants that depend on them and the triggers that reopen them.
- Trigger events emit a reconsideration record with the observation that fired them.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-14)
[ ] Each policy states its assumptions, expiry, and review triggers.
[ ] Grant-to-policy links are recorded and current.
[ ] Fired triggers show the resulting grant state changes and reviewer decisions.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-14)
Trigger review when a material change in the evidence left the policy and its dependent grants untouched.

artifacts.name: Policy record template
artifacts.purpose: Version, assumptions, evidence, expiry, triggers, and dependent grants in one record.

artifacts.name: Trigger catalog
artifacts.purpose: The observations and thresholds that reopen a policy, with the owner of each.

artifacts.name: Reconsideration log
artifacts.purpose: What fired, which grants moved, who reviewed, and what was decided.

example.title: Reopening an eligibility rule after a population shift
example.description: A benefits team gives its eligibility policy a 12-month expiry and a trigger on a five-point shift in applicant mix; when the shift lands, the two grants that cite the policy move to review_required and the reviewer renews one and narrows the other.

antiPatterns.title: Policy as ground truth
antiPatterns.failure: The policy is treated as a fixed input consumed at deployment, so changed facts never reach the authority that rests on it.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Policy is a versioned state with assumptions, expiry, and triggers that can move grants.
antiPatterns.warning: A policy can be long-lived; what it may not be is unreviewable.

antiPatterns.title: Triggers with no destination
antiPatterns.failure: Alerts fire on the metric but nothing in the authority state changes.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: A fired trigger moves the dependent grants and produces a reconsideration record.
antiPatterns.warning: A reviewer may leave the grant in place; the record of that decision is the point.

entries.title: MEC-15 Withdrawal rehearsal
entries.summary: Run the workflow without the system on a schedule and measure what withdrawal would cost at the technical, operational, and institutional levels.
cues: Rehearse the workflow without the system rather than testing that the switch flips.
Measure cost, the expertise still available, and time to restore at each reversibility level.
Record which capacities have to be preserved to keep the rehearsal possible next year.
steps: Pick a bounded slice of the workflow and run it without the system for a defined window.
Record the cost, the people who still hold the expertise, and the time to restore service at the technical, operational, and institutional levels.
Publish the gaps as preserved capacities with owners and a date for the next rehearsal.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-15 Withdrawal rehearsal)
- Rehearse operating the workflow without the system on a published schedule.
- Record cost, expertise available, and time to restore at the technical, operational, and institutional levels.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/withdrawal-rehearsal
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-15)
- The system supports a rehearsal mode that suspends automated handling for a defined scope and window.
- Rehearsal outcomes are recorded against the dependency record for the workflow.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-15)
[ ] Rehearsals ran on schedule with a defined scope and window.
[ ] Results state cost, expertise available, and time to restore at all three levels.
[ ] Preserved capacities have named owners and review dates.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-15)
Trigger review when a rehearsal is skipped, or when it shows the workflow can no longer be run without the system.

artifacts.name: Rehearsal plan
artifacts.purpose: Scope, window, participants, and the measures to be taken during the exercise.

artifacts.name: Three-level reversibility readout
artifacts.purpose: Cost and time to restore recorded separately for technical, operational, and institutional withdrawal.

artifacts.name: Preserved capacity list
artifacts.purpose: The staffing, tooling, and knowledge that must be maintained for withdrawal to stay possible, with owners.

example.title: A week of manual triage
example.description: A claims team runs one region manually for a week each quarter, finds that throughput halves and that only two reviewers still hold the rules, and funds a training rotation as a preserved capacity.

antiPatterns.title: The switch exists
antiPatterns.failure: A documented kill switch is treated as proof of reversibility, though nobody has run the workflow without the system in years.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Withdrawal is rehearsed on a schedule and the cost of doing it is measured.
antiPatterns.warning: A rehearsal can be scoped to a slice of traffic; what it may not be is hypothetical.

antiPatterns.title: Rehearsal without a record
antiPatterns.failure: The drill happens but produces no measurement, so nothing can be compared to last year.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each rehearsal records cost, expertise, and restore time against the dependency record.
antiPatterns.warning: Qualitative findings are useful, but at least one comparable measure has to survive the exercise.

entries.title: MEC-16 Intervention specification
entries.summary: Replace the human-in-the-loop checkbox with a specification of who intervenes, what they can see, what they can prevent or alter, and what happens when they disagree.
cues: State what the intervener can see at the moment of the decision, not afterward.
Separate what they can prevent from what they can alter after the fact.
Write down what happens when the human disagrees with the system.
steps: Name the intervention owner and the decisions they cover.
Record the information available, the actions preventable, the states alterable, and the on-disagreement path.
Record the incentives acting on the intervener, the cost of intervening, and the time it takes them to reach the decision.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-16 Intervention specification)
- Any control described as human oversight is documented as an intervention specification with owner, information available, actions preventable, states alterable, and on-disagreement path.
- The specification records the incentives, the cost of intervening, and the time to reach the decision.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/intervention-specification
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-16)
- The interface presents the intervener with the information the specification names, before the action commits.
- Disagreement is a recorded outcome with a route, not an unlogged override.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-16)
[ ] Every claimed oversight control has a current intervention specification.
[ ] Reach time and cost of intervening are measured, not asserted.
[ ] Disagreement outcomes are logged with what changed as a result.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-16)
Trigger review when a decision described as human-reviewed proceeded without the reviewer being able to alter it.

artifacts.name: Intervention specification template
artifacts.purpose: Owner, information, preventable actions, alterable states, disagreement path, incentives, cost, and reach time.

artifacts.name: Reach-time measurement
artifacts.purpose: Observed time between the trigger and the intervener being in a position to act.

artifacts.name: Disagreement log
artifacts.purpose: Cases where the intervener disagreed, what route it took, and what changed.

example.title: Specifying review on an automated suspension
example.description: A trust and safety team documents that the on-call reviewer sees the evidence and the account history, can prevent suspension for 30 minutes, can reverse it for 14 days, and that disagreement routes to a policy owner within one business day.

antiPatterns.title: Rubber-stamp review
antiPatterns.failure: A human approves in bulk without the information or the time to alter the outcome, and the approval is counted as oversight.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The specification states what the reviewer sees, what they can change, and how long they have.
antiPatterns.warning: High approval rates are not proof of rubber-stamping; the test is whether refusal was possible and reachable.

antiPatterns.title: Oversight named but not scoped
antiPatterns.failure: Policy says a human is in the loop without saying which decisions, which states, or which disagreement path.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each oversight claim resolves to a specification covering named decisions.
antiPatterns.warning: One specification can cover a class of decisions if the class is stated.

entries.title: MEC-17 Capability catalog
entries.summary: List what a system could do separately from the register of what it is permitted to do, so knowing a capability never grants it.
cues: Let discovery answer what is possible; let the grant register answer what is permitted.
Record how each capability was tested, and when.
Refuse an ungranted action by naming the capability and the missing grant.
steps: Catalog the actions the assembled system can perform, including those reachable through tools and sub-agents.
Record for each capability how it was verified and when that verification expires.
Serve the catalog on a read path that carries no authority, and refuse execution unless a grant is in the allowed state.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-17 Capability catalog)
- Maintain a catalog of what the assembled system can do, separate from the register of what it is permitted to do.
- Discovery of a capability confers no authority; execution requires a grant in the allowed state.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/capability-catalog
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-17)
- Capability discovery succeeds for actions the system cannot lawfully perform.
- A refusal names the capability, the required grant, and the grant's current state.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-17)
[ ] The catalog lists capabilities reachable through tools and sub-agents.
[ ] Each capability records its verification method and date.
[ ] Attempts to execute ungranted capabilities are refused and logged.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-17)
Trigger review when a newly reachable capability was exercised without a grant being issued for it.

artifacts.name: Capability record template
artifacts.purpose: Action, surface, preconditions, verification method, and verification date.

artifacts.name: Discovery endpoint contract
artifacts.purpose: Read-only interface that returns capabilities and their grant status without granting anything.

artifacts.name: Refusal message pattern
artifacts.purpose: Standard wording that cites the capability, the required grant, and its state.

example.title: An agent that can see the payout tool it may not use
example.description: An operations agent discovers the payout tool in the catalog, reads that the matching grant is in review_required, refuses the action citing the grant identifier and state, and files a request for authorization instead.

antiPatterns.title: Discover equals permit
antiPatterns.failure: Anything the system can reach is treated as something it may do, so capability growth silently widens authority.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Discovery and authorization are separate surfaces, and execution checks the grant.
antiPatterns.warning: Hiding a capability is not a substitute for refusing it; a hidden capability that executes is still ungoverned.

antiPatterns.title: Catalog without verification
antiPatterns.failure: Capabilities are listed from documentation, so the catalog describes intent rather than what the system can do.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Each entry records how the capability was tested and when.
antiPatterns.warning: Verification can be sampled; the record should say which entries are asserted rather than tested.

entries.title: MEC-18 Dependency ledger
entries.summary: Track who now depends on the system, what substitution would cost, which expertise remains, and which capacities are being preserved to keep withdrawal possible.
cues: Treat dependence as a state variable that moves, not as a background condition.
Record alternatives while they still exist, not once they are gone.
Give every preserved capacity an owner and a budget line.
steps: List the dependents on the workflow, inside and outside the organization.
Record substitution cost, the expertise retained, and the alternatives that still exist, and derive an exposure score.
Name the preserved capacities with owners and review the ledger on the same cadence as the safety case.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-18 Dependency ledger)
- Maintain a dependency ledger with dependents, substitution cost, expertise retained, alternatives, and an exposure score.
- Name the capacities preserved to keep withdrawal possible, each with an owner.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/dependency-ledger
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-18)
- Exposure score and its inputs are reported alongside reliability metrics.
- Changes in dependents or alternatives update the ledger within the review cycle.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-18)
[ ] Dependents are listed with the consequence of an outage for each.
[ ] Substitution cost, expertise retained, and alternatives are recorded and dated.
[ ] Preserved capacities have owners and evidence they are still funded.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-18)
Trigger review when exposure rises materially without a corresponding change in preserved capacity.

artifacts.name: Dependency record template
artifacts.purpose: Dependents, substitution cost, expertise retained, alternatives, and exposure score.

artifacts.name: Exposure score worksheet
artifacts.purpose: How depth of dependence, substitution cost, and correction latency combine into the score.

artifacts.name: Preserved capacity register
artifacts.purpose: Capacities kept alive for withdrawal, with owners, budget, and review dates.

example.title: Ledger for a scheduling system three years in
example.description: A hospital records that two departments have retired their manual roster, that the last two schedulers who could rebuild it retire next year, and funds a documented fallback roster as a preserved capacity.

antiPatterns.title: Reliability as safety
antiPatterns.failure: High uptime is read as low risk, while the institution's ability to work without the system quietly disappears.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Dependence is tracked separately from reliability, with its own score and owners.
antiPatterns.warning: A reliable system can be a safe one; the ledger asks a different question, which is what happens when it is gone.

antiPatterns.title: Ledger without alternatives
antiPatterns.failure: Dependents are recorded but substitutes are never checked, so the entry cannot show when the last alternative disappeared.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Alternatives are rechecked on the review cadence and dated.
antiPatterns.warning: Having no alternative is a legitimate finding as long as it is recorded as one.

entries.title: MEC-19 Expansion review
entries.summary: Make scope growth its own authorization decision, with fresh evidence and a check that correction capacity grew with it.
cues: Treat a successful pilot as a request to expand, not as an approval to expand.
Ask what correction capacity the wider scope needs before the scope moves.
Record expansion as a transition on the grant, with its own evidence.
steps: Define what counts as expansion for this system: new population, new action class, higher ceiling, or lower attendance.
Require an expansion record with the evidence for the wider scope and the correction capacity it will need.
Record the decision as an expansion transition on the grant, or refuse it and say what evidence is missing.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-19 Expansion review)
- Any growth in population, action class, ceiling, or autonomy is authorized as a new decision with its own evidence.
- The decision records whether correction capacity grows with the expanded scope.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/expansion-review
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-19)
- Scope changes are applied through a grant transition, not through configuration drift.
- The grant history distinguishes expansion transitions from renewals.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-19)
[ ] Expansion criteria are defined for the system.
[ ] Each expansion has a record with evidence and a correction-capacity check.
[ ] Grant histories show expansion transitions with reviewers.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-19)
Trigger review when scope grew without an expansion record, or when it grew while correction capacity stayed fixed.

artifacts.name: Expansion record template
artifacts.purpose: Proposed scope change, evidence for it, and the correction capacity it requires.

artifacts.name: Correction capacity check
artifacts.purpose: Comparison of the reviewers, reversal paths, and repair budget before and after the change.

artifacts.name: Expansion criteria list
artifacts.purpose: What counts as expansion for this system, agreed before the first request.

example.title: From one region to all regions
example.description: A pilot that ran well in one region is treated as a request rather than a result: the team files an expansion record, finds the appeals queue would need two more reviewers, funds them, and only then transitions the grant.

antiPatterns.title: The automation ratchet
antiPatterns.failure: Success is taken as its own authorization, so scope only ever widens and never contracts.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Expansion is a decision with evidence, and contraction is an available outcome.
antiPatterns.warning: Fast expansion is fine when each step is a recorded decision with capacity behind it.

antiPatterns.title: Expansion by configuration
antiPatterns.failure: Scope grows through a threshold change or a new tool binding that no one reviews as an authority change.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Scope changes move through a grant transition with a reviewer.
antiPatterns.warning: Routine parameter tuning inside an agreed ceiling is not expansion; crossing the ceiling is.

entries.title: MEC-21 Halt tier register
entries.summary: Tier halt authority by blast radius so the power to stop scales with the size of what is being stopped, and the smallest tiers stay cheap enough to use.
cues: Rank halt instruments by blast radius: one case, one queue, one workflow, the whole system.
Name who can fire each tier and what restoration at that tier requires.
Keep the lowest tier unescalated: a frontline pause that needs a committee is not a tier; it is theater.
steps: List the halt instruments the deployment has today and sort them by blast radius, restoration cost, and who can reach them.
Write the tier register: per tier, the authorized roles, what halts, the restoration path, the notification duty, and the evidence the halt leaves behind.
Provision restoration at every tier and rehearse at least the bottom two, where halts are cheap enough that drills are honest.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-21 Halt tier register)
- Halt authority is tiered by blast radius, with authorized roles, restoration paths, and notification duties recorded per tier.
- The lowest tier is reachable by exposed parties and frontline operators without escalation.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/halt-tier-register
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-21)
- Each tier exposes only the controls that tier's blast radius justifies.
- Halt events record the tier that fired, the restoration path taken, and everyone notified.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-21)
[ ] The tier register exists and names roles, blast radius, restoration, and notification per tier.
[ ] Drills demonstrate halts at the lowest tiers, not only the system-wide stop.
[ ] Restoration capacity is evidenced at each tier, not only at the top.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-21)
Trigger review when a halt had to escalate two or more tiers to take effect, or when a tier's restoration path was exercised without provision behind it.

artifacts.name: Halt tier register
artifacts.purpose: Tiers, authorized roles, blast radius, restoration paths, and notification duties per tier.

artifacts.name: Tier drill log
artifacts.purpose: Evidence that low tiers fire and restore without escalation, dated and signed.

artifacts.name: Escalation map
artifacts.purpose: What happens when a tier is insufficient, and who holds the next tier up.

example.title: One caseworker, one paused claim
example.description: A caseworker pauses a single claim the system is about to mispay, using a tier-1 control that needs no approval. The queue keeps moving; the claim routes to a human; the register records the pause and the restoration, and nobody outside the office is paged.

antiPatterns.title: One halt authority for every tier
antiPatterns.failure: Every halt requires the same senior authority, so low-tier problems either wait or fire the system-wide stop.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Tiers match blast radius: small halts are cheap and local; big halts are deliberate.
antiPatterns.warning: A small authorized tier is not a governance gap; the gap is a big tier with no rehearsed restoration.

antiPatterns.title: Tier theater
antiPatterns.failure: Tiers exist on paper, but the low tiers route through the same approver as the top, so blast radius never changes who decides.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Authorized roles differ per tier, and drill logs show low-tier halts completing without escalation.
antiPatterns.warning: Shared approval across tiers is legitimate when coverage is explicit, not when it is an accident of hierarchy.

entries.title: MEC-22 Admission gate
entries.summary: Treat the decision to deploy at all as an authorization, with evidence and a recorded outcome. Choosing not to deploy is a valid result.
cues: Review admission before the grant exists, not as a post-hoc audit of a running system.
Record the refusal basis when the answer is no, and make "not yet" and "never" distinguishable.
Give the refusal a review condition, so a no made on stale evidence can be reopened on named facts.
steps: Before any grant is written, run the admission review: evidence for the delegation, the scope considered, the correction capacity available, and the populations affected.
Record the outcome as a decision with a named decider, including deliberate non-use with reasons.
Attach a review condition to every admission, so changed facts reopen the question instead of aging into acceptance.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-22 Admission gate)
- A consequential deployment has a recorded admission decision with evidence, scope, and a named decider, before any authority is granted.
- Deliberate non-use is a recorded outcome with reasons and a review condition.
Reference: https://ethotechnics.org/mechanisms/patterns/admission-gate
entries.productRequirement:
Product requirement (MEC-22)
- The admission decision is a prerequisite artifact in the deployment pipeline, not a document written after launch.
- The record distinguishes "not yet" from "never", with different reopen conditions.
entries.auditEvidenceChecklist:
Audit evidence checklist (MEC-22)
[ ] Every consequential deployment traces to an admission decision with a decider and a date.
[ ] Refusals record their basis and a review condition.
[ ] Systems running without a recordable admission decision are listed as findings.
entries.postmortemTrigger:
Postmortem trigger (MEC-22)
Trigger review when a deployment is found to be running with no admission record, or when an admission refusal was reopened by momentum rather than by the review condition.

artifacts.name: Admission decision record
artifacts.purpose: Evidence reviewed, scope considered, correction capacity, affected populations, outcome, and decider.

artifacts.name: Non-use record
artifacts.purpose: Reasons a delegation was refused or deferred, with the review condition that can reopen it.

artifacts.name: Admission criteria list
artifacts.purpose: What the gate asks, agreed before the first request so the bar cannot move to fit the answer.

example.title: The pilot that was declined
example.description: A fraud-scoring model is proposed for benefits triage. The admission review finds the correction capacity for the denial class is absent and the affected population cannot reach a responder inside the clock. The outcome is recorded as non-use with those reasons and a reopen condition: the gate reopens when a funded responder path exists, not when the vendor updates the model.

antiPatterns.title: Admission by momentum
antiPatterns.failure: The system runs because someone built it, and stopping now is more expensive than starting was, so the question is never asked.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: The admission decision exists with a date, a decider, and evidence taken before the grant.
antiPatterns.warning: A small pilot still needs a recorded admission; the record is what makes expansion a decision later.

antiPatterns.title: Gate as rubber stamp
antiPatterns.failure: Every review passes because the criteria were written after the first request, fitted to the answer wanted.
antiPatterns.counterfactual: Admission criteria are agreed and published before the first request reaches them.
antiPatterns.warning: A no that cannot be given is not a gate; audit the refusals, not only the approvals.

entries.title: MEC-23 Challenge load ledger
entries.summary: Track challenge volume against response capacity, so sustained congestion triggers a resourcing or scope decision instead of a narrowing of who may challenge.
cues: Report challenge volume, response capacity, and unanswered-challenge age as one series.
Tie sustained breaches of response clocks to a recorded resourcing or scope decision.
Never meet congestion by narrowing standing; meet it by capacity or by emitting less error.
steps: Instrument the challenge path: volume, response latency, unanswered-challenge age, and the response capacity rostered to answer.
Define the congestion threshold where a breach obliges a capacity or scope decision, and record which decision was made.
Review the ledger on the same cadence as the standing register, so density and eligibility are never adjusted in isolation.
entries.policyRequirement:
Policy requirement (MEC-23 Challenge load ledger)
